title: Weiss v. United States, with Hernandez v. United States
citation: 510 U.S. 163 (1994), with Hernandez v. United States
lead: Two Marines challenge the appointment and tenure of the judges who heard their criminal cases, prompting the Court to distinguish military assignments from new constitutional offices.

actors.name: Weiss
actors.role: Marine convicted by guilty plea of larceny.

actors.name: Hernandez
actors.role: Marine convicted by guilty plea of cocaine offenses and conspiracy.

actors.name: Judge Advocates General
actors.role: Service officials assigning already commissioned officers to military judicial work.

proceedings: The Navy-Marine Corps Court of Military Review affirmed each conviction.
The Court of Military Appeals rejected Weiss’s structural challenges and affirmed Hernandez by reliance on that decision.
The Supreme Court affirmed both judgments unanimously in result, with several separate rationales.
limits: The judges in these cases were already presidentially appointed and Senate-confirmed military officers. Civilian appellate judges, actual bias, and current military law were not adjudicated; the Court did not retry pleas or alter sentences.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Weiss and Hernandez plead guilty before military courts
sections.cue: What sentences and appellate decisions preceded their constitutional challenges?
paragraphs: Weiss, a Marine, pleaded guilty to larceny at a special court-martial. His sentence included three months in confinement, partial forfeiture of pay, and a bad-conduct discharge. Another Marine, Hernandez, pleaded guilty to cocaine possession, importation, distribution, and conspiracy. His sentence included twenty-five years’ confinement, total pay forfeiture, rank reduction, and dishonorable discharge; the convening authority reduced confinement to twenty years.

The Navy-Marine Corps Court of Military Review separately affirmed. Weiss challenged military trial and appellate judges because Judge Advocates General selected them without new Appointments Clause appointments and because they lacked fixed terms. The Court of Military Appeals rejected both arguments. Two judges found existing commissions sufficient, one regarded the Clause as inapplicable to the military, and two separately dissented. The court affirmed Hernandez on the strength of Weiss’s decision. The two petitioners sought joint Supreme Court review.

sections.title: Rehnquist examines what offices and appointments the judges already held
sections.cue: Why were special legal qualifications not conclusive?
paragraphs: Chief Justice Rehnquist’s opinion described trial judges as commissioned officers with appropriate bar membership, selected and certified by the relevant Judge Advocate General and detailed to courts-martial. Appellate judges could be officers or civilians, but every judge in these cases was already a military officer appointed by the President with Senate consent. The civilian-appellate issue was expressly outside the case.

The parties agreed that military judges performed constitutional-officer responsibilities and that the Appointments Clause applied to military officers. The question was a second appointment, not exemption from Article II. Bar membership did not itself establish a separate office; pilots and military lawyers also needed qualifications beyond ordinary commissions.

Congress expressly required additional presidential appointment and confirmation for some senior posts but used assignment and detail for military judges. The Court would not infer an intended second appointment that Congress simply failed to provide. Buckley, Freytag, and Morrison showed that the positions involved officers, but did not answer when an existing officer needed reappointment.

sources.pinpoint: Military judging as assignment; 510 U.S. at 167–73 & nn.2–5

sections.title: Judicial discipline duties fit the military office under an assumed germaneness test
sections.cue: What did the majority leave undecided about that test?
paragraphs: Shoemaker allowed germane duties to be assigned to existing officers. The Court distinguished its designation of two identifiable incumbents from an indefinite set of military judges chosen among many qualified officers. Congress had not selected a particular individual and thereby evaded the appointments process.

The majority nevertheless assumed, without conclusively deciding, that germaneness governed and found it satisfied. Officers historically maintained discipline, arrested personnel, administered lawful nonjudicial punishment, served on courts-martial, and reviewed sentences. Military judges lacked independent general judicial authority apart from assigned courts, could return to other duties, and with permission could perform nonjudicial work while serving as trial judges. These features differed from a full-time civilian judicial office.

The judges’ existing constitutional commissions therefore sufficed; neither the statute nor the Clause required another appointment for this work. The majority’s reservation about the necessity of germaneness matters alongside its conclusion that the duties were germane.

sections.title: The Court evaluates impartiality without treating fixed tenure as indispensable
sections.cue: Which present safeguards accompanied the historical practice?
paragraphs: The petitioners sought a fixed term rather than Article III life tenure and alleged no actual or apparent bias in their judges. Their claim was structural: absence of tenure necessarily destroyed sufficient independence. The Court accepted impartial adjudication as basic due process but gave particular weight to Congress’s military authority. Under Middendorf it asked whether the factors favoring fixed terms were extraordinarily weighty enough to overcome Congress’s balance, rather than importing Mathews or Medina unchanged.

Military courts had long operated without tenured judges, Congress’s revisions had not imposed fixed terms for these trial and intermediate appellate roles, and a 1983 commission recommended against guaranteed terms. History was relevant but did not automatically validate every inherited procedure.

Contemporary safeguards also mattered. Judge Advocates General supervised judges, while the military justice code barred command authorities from evaluating or censuring adjudicative work. Judges could not hear cases in which they previously participated; accused persons could challenge for cause and learn the judge’s identity before choosing judge-alone trial. The civilian Court of Military Appeals, whose judges had fifteen-year terms, enforced prohibitions on evaluation, decertification, or transfer based on disagreement with findings or sentences.
Those rules defeated the premise of unfettered removal power. Together with history, they left the requested tenure protection insufficiently weighty to override Congress’s arrangement.

sections.title: Souter and Ginsburg explain qualifications to their agreement
sections.cue: Why did officer status and constitutional scrutiny still matter?
paragraphs: Justice Souter joined on the understanding that military judges were inferior officers. Presidential appointment with Senate consent can be used for inferior offices and does not automatically make every commissioned officer principal. But assignment of principal responsibilities by a lower official from a broad pool might evade the required principal-officer appointment process. Constitutional safeguards prevent abdication as well as one branch’s aggrandizement.

He found the classification debatable, especially for appellate judges, but regarded review of trial decisions, reassignment authority, and lack of fixed terms as relevant limitations. In a close case he would accept a fully rational political-branch judgment and classified these officers as inferior. His concurrence did not settle the status of Tax Court judges or add a Court holding on every classification question.

Justice Ginsburg emphasized that servicemembers retain constitutional rights. Modern military justice had improved on its predecessors, but the claims still deserved scrutiny. The Court’s examination of present safeguards respected that obligation.

sources.pinpoint: Souter and Ginsburg concurrences; 510 U.S. at 182–95 and Souter nn.1–9

sections.title: Scalia and Thomas insist on germaneness but regard settled tradition as sufficient on tenure
sections.cue: How did their route differ from the majority’s?
paragraphs: Justice Scalia, joined by Thomas, thought germaneness necessary whenever someone outside the Clause’s permitted appointing authorities assigned duties amounting to a new office. A Judge Advocate General was not such an appointing authority. Scalia upheld these assignments because the duties were germane, criticizing the suggestion that a large pool of possible assignees might make that inquiry unnecessary. His note viewed Souter’s principal-versus-inferior issues as insufficiently presented.

On due process, Scalia and Thomas found the accepted military tradition sufficient and rejected judicial rebalancing of independence and accountability. They expressly distinguished civilian judicial tenure; their position did not license civilian criminal judges to serve at executive pleasure.

sources.pinpoint: Scalia concurrence; 510 U.S. at 195–99 and starred note

sections.title: Both convictions survive the structural objections without new sentencing decisions
sections.cue: Which portions of the opinion had which support?
paragraphs: On January 19, 1994, the Supreme Court affirmed both military appellate judgments. All nine agreed with the result. Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg joined Rehnquist throughout. Scalia and Thomas joined Part I on appointments and Part II-A on tenure history, reaching the rest of the result through their separate reasoning.

The Court neither retried guilty pleas nor revised sentences. The appointed officers could perform these germane judicial duties without another appointment, and the existing military safeguards did not require fixed terms. The court names and procedures describe the 1994 system; later changes and civilian military-appellate appointments require separate analysis.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment and alignment; Assigned scope; 510 U.S. at 164, 181–99
